# Representation and Kernel Modifications

Also called: Kernel Variants, Primitive Attribute Modifications, Geometric Regularization in 3DGS

## Overview
Representation and Kernel Modifications extend the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework by altering the primitive attributes, the kernel functions used for opacity estimation, or the geometric constraints applied during optimization [S1, S2]. While standard 3DGS relies on isotropic/anisotropic Gaussians with positive colors and exponential kernels, this family introduces negative colors for high-frequency modeling, voxel-based scaffolding for attribute prediction, tangent-plane densification for geometric smoothness, alternative Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) for rendering efficiency, and grid-based blur kernels for defocus modeling [S1, S2]. These methods address specific limitations such as noisy geometry, limited expressivity of the Gaussian kernel, or the need for watertight surface reconstruction.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate within the differentiable rasterization pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent](3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md). They share the core data structure of Gaussian primitives defined by mean position $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ (or rotation/scale), opacity $\alpha$, and color $\mathbf{c}$ (often represented by spherical harmonics coefficients). The rendering equation remains the standard alpha compositing formula:
$$ C = \sum_{i \in N} c_i \alpha_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j) $$
where $\alpha_i$ is derived from a kernel function $K(d_M)$ of the Mahalanobis distance $d_M$ [S1]. The optimization loop uses gradient descent to minimize a photometric loss (e.g., L1 or L2) between rendered and ground-truth images, often augmented with task-specific regularization or structural constraints [S1, S2].

## Subtopics

### [Negative Gaussian Splatting](9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md)
Negative Gaussian Splatting (NegGS) extends the 3DGS primitive structure by allowing Gaussians with negative color values. The scene is represented by a joint family $G_{NeGS} = G_{GS} \cup G_{-GS}$, where $G_{GS}$ contains positive colors and $G_{-GS}$ contains negative colors. This enables "cancellation" effects, modeling Diff-Gaussians (difference of Gaussians) to represent sharper features and complex nonlinear structures. The optimal coefficient $c_{opt}$ for two Gaussians $f_{m_0, \Sigma_0}$ and $f_{m_1, \Sigma_1}$ minimizes the ratio of their densities at a null density vector $w$, defined by $\Sigma_1^{-1}(w - m_1) = \Sigma_0^{-1}(w - m_0)$. For diagonal covariances, $w_i = (m_{1,i} - h_i m_{0,i})/(1 - h_i)$ if $h_i < 1$. A negative mask tracks negative Gaussians. Initialization sets approximately 20% of Gaussians as negative. Choose this when high-frequency color details or complex nonlinear structures are present.

### [Scaffold-GS](9186-scaffold-gs.md)
Scaffold-GS replaces direct storage of Gaussian attributes with a structured, voxel-based representation. A voxel grid is initialized with learnable feature vectors $\mathbf{f}_v$. Gaussian attributes (color, opacity, covariance) are predicted by interpolating features from surrounding voxels $V_i$ via $\mathbf{F}_i = \sum_{v \in V_i} w_{i,v} \mathbf{f}_v$ and passing $\mathbf{F}_i$ through lightweight MLPs. This decouples the geometric scaffold from primitive attributes, improving generalization in sparse regions. Choose this when memory efficiency or attribute prediction stability is required.

### [GeoGaussian](9187-geogaussian.md)
GeoGaussian improves geometric consistency by modifying densification and initialization. New Gaussians are spawned on the tangent plane of a parent Gaussian $G_p$ ($\mu_{new} = \mu_p + v, v \cdot n_p = 0$) to ensure alignment. A normal consistency loss $L_{smooth} = \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{N}} (1 - n_i \cdot n_j)$ penalizes discontinuities between neighbors. Plane constraints may also be applied. Choose this when surface smoothness and geometric coherence are prioritized over raw appearance fidelity.

### [DARBF-Splatting](9911-darbf-splatting.md)
DARBF-Splatting replaces the exponential Gaussian kernel with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions (DARBFs). Kernels include Half-Cosine ($\cos(d_M^2/\xi)$ for $d_M^2 < \xi \pi/2$) and Inverse Multiquadric. These span larger regions with higher opacity for the same variance, reducing primitive count and memory usage by up to 15% and accelerating convergence by 34%. A scalar correction factor $\psi$ is applied to the kernel output to approximate the closed-form integration property of Gaussians, avoiding costly integration. Choose this for faster training and lower memory footprint.

### [Grid-based Blur Kernel](14244-grid-based-blur-kernel.md)
Grid-based Blur Kernels replace MLP-generated blur kernels with a learnable grid $\mathcal{B}$ of shape $\mathbb{R}^{N_{img} \times N_k \times K \times K \times C}$ indexed by sharpness level. A sharpness level map $L$ is precomputed from a Defocus Map Estimation Network. For each pixel, the corresponding kernel is retrieved and convolved with the local image patch. This allows spatially-varying blurriness modeling with capacity scaling via grid size without extra kernel generation cost. Choose this for scenes with significant defocus or blur.

### Gaussian Shell Maps
Gaussian Shell Maps (GSMs) combine CNN-based generators with 3DGS to recreate virtual humans with sophisticated details such as clothing and accessories [S1].

### Gaussian Wrapping
Gaussian Wrapping reinterprets 3D Gaussian primitives as oriented probabilistic surface elements representing geometry only within an oriented half-space [S2]. The Gaussian models density decay on the outward-facing side, while the inward-facing side is fully occupied [S2]. A learnable oriented normal is introduced, enabling closed-form expressions for occupancy, vacancy, and normal fields [S2]. Geometric gaps are identified and densified to form a watertight shell [S2]. A consistency loss and dedicated densification strategy enforce wrapping [S2]. The rasterizer outputs depth as an isosurface, and Primal Adaptive Meshing extracts meshes [S2]. ## Background
3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. [Parent](3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md). Subsequent works modified the representation to address limitations in geometry, kernel expressivity, and rendering efficiency. Negative Gaussian Splatting, Scaffold-GS, GeoGaussian, DARBF-Splatting, and Grid-based Blur Kernels are detailed in [S1]. Gaussian Wrapping is detailed in [S2]. Gaussian Shell Maps are mentioned in [S1] as part of the broader landscape of human reconstruction methods.
